newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Beach to boost oil output.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Beach to boost oil output.

text.p: Beach Petroleum NL aims to double oil production to around 800,000 barrels a year and start bringing gas volumes onstream over the next two to three years as it finally emerges from its crippling corporate woes.

In an interview with Reuters, Beach chief executive Reg Nelson said the company would focus on existing and increasing acreage in the Cooper and Eromanga basins in South Australia and Queensland to provide a solid platform of growth and cashflow as the basis for further exploration offshore and in Asia.
The company also has high hopes for its 6.36 percent stake in the Pandora offshore gas field in the Gulf of Papua, and its East Korean Bay Production Sharing Concession in North Korea.

Beach reported a A$2.7 million net profit for 1995/96, boosted by the recovery of around A$13 million through settlements from its involvement in the 1980s in the Independent Resources (IRL) group, which was the subject of extensive investigations and prosecutions in the wake of in-house deals.
In the company's annual report, Nelson said 1995/96 had transformed Beach Petroleum "from a company ravaged by fraud into an oil and gas explorer with solid working capital".
Nelson told Reuters that Beach still had the potential to recover up to A$60 million through continuing litigation, but this was not crucial to the future of the company which was now debt-free.
"With increased production from Kenmore and Bodalla in particular, we should be well towards making an operating profit in the first six months of this financial year," he said.
Total oil production in 1996/97 was likely to maintained at the 1995/96 level of around 383,000 barrels, he said.

Beach believes there is good potential for further discoveries at Thylungra in southwest Queensland, where it has a 19.6 percent stake in the Oil Co of Australia Ltd operation, where tests have demonstrated a rich condensate to gas ratio.

Nelson is also optimistic about its eight percent stake in ATP 548P to the north, adjacent the Inland Oil Field, where the Taipan oil prospect is due for drilling in December, and about Beach's gas prospects in the Arrowie Basin, which lie alongside the gas and liquids pipelines from Moomba to Adelaide.

Beach has aggressively bid for increasing acreage in the Cooper/Eromanga in Queensland this year, and recently moved its headquarters to Adelaide from Sydney to position itself for the opening up of strategic permits in South Australia in 1999.

Having already disposed of gold mining and exploration assets acquired through affiliate Spargos Mining NL, Nelson said Beach could possibly sell out of its U.S. oil holding, the South Burbanks oil block in Oklahoma, where costs had been cut dramatically, but production and earnings remained low.
The block was not strategic, but Beach is planning seismic surveys beneath the shallow Burbank sands before considering further options which could include divestment, he said.

Nelson said the company remained excited about its East Korean Bay venture, where it is entering into a farm-in agreement with Malaysia's Puspita Emas Sdn Bhd, and planned seismic surveys in the area in March or April next year.
"We have got exposure there to what we think is a very high reward, even though it might be high risk," he said.

Nelson said with the current offshore interest in Australia's strategically placed oil and gas companies, it was "always possible" that Beach could be a takeover target, however he believed it had a degree of stability in the share register.
While Beach itself did not have any corporate acqusitions in mind, it remained interested in asset acqusitions, particularly in the Cooper and Eromanga basins, he said.
Nelson said he believed market interest in Beach had tapered off in 1995/96 "because we were not in the drilling activity we thought we would be in because of problems getting rigs and approvals."
"I certainly recognise we need to get out with a much more aggressive programme and we are certainly working on it," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
